question.leadin: Identify some of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
question.text: King Nebuchadnezzar ("NEB-uh-kud-NEZZ-ur") of Chaldea ("cal-DEE-uh") built these structures for his wife Amytis ("AM-uh-tis") of Media. They consisted of terraces and irrigation structures that serviced a variety of luscious trees.
question.clue: According to Strabo, an early version of Archimedes' Screw was built for use at this location.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about Mesopotamian empires and emperors.
swap.text: This ruler of the Babylonian Empire consolidated his power and defeated Rim-Sin of Lagash. His namesake law code included the ruling "an eye for an eye".
swap.clue: This Amorite king went up a mountain to receive a stele from the sun god Shamash that was later discovered in Susa.

question.text: The Sumerians invented textbooks while teaching scribes this Mesopotamian writing system at the eduba. This writing system was designed for reeds to be pressed into clay tablets.
question.clue: Henry Rawlinson studied the Behistun Inscription for insight into this system, which is seen on the oldest complaint tablet.

swap.text: This Mesopotamiam civilization is the earliest known human civilization. This civilization, whose city-states included Ur, developed the cuneiform writing system.
swap.clue: This civilization was the first to farm year-round by employing irrigation canals, and its priesthood worshipped Anu and Inanna.

question.leadin: This ancient eastern empire was a vassal state under two large empires during different times of its existence.
question.text: Name this empire, with capital was Nineveh (NIN-uh-vuh). Its rulers included Sennacherib (suh-NA-kuh-rib) and Ashurbanipal (a-shur-BAA-nuh-paal).
question.clue: Accounts of invasions by this empire written by king Taharqa record that its armies had their bowstrings eaten by field mice.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the reign of Tiglath-Pileser III.
swap.text: Tiglath-Pileser ruled the "neo-" version of this empire, whose other leaders included Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal.
swap.clue: This empire's final defeat came when Harran fell, an act precipitated by the civil war that broke out between Sin-shar-ishkun and Ashur-etel-ilani.

question.leadin: This was the first empire of the ancient world.
question.text: Name this empire which reached its peak under Naram-Sin and fell to the Gutian invasions. The Elamites wererivals of this empire.
question.clue: Its most famous ruler's life was detailed on the Ebla tablets, and started out as a cup-bearer to Ur-Zababa of Kish.

swap.text: Leonard and Katherine Woolley excavated several royal tombs in this Sumerian city-state. This city's Ziggurat (ZI-gur-aht) was discovered by John George Taylor.
swap.clue: A king named -Nammu, who founded a dynasty that supplanted Lagash and the Gutians, was succeeded by Shulgi.

question.leadin: Name some of the users of ceramics in the ancient world.
question.text: This ancient civilization used clay for building, for tablets on which they invented writing in the form of cuneiform, and for pottery, for which they invented the wheel.
question.clue: The last king of the Lagash dynasty, Lugal-Zage-Si was the last king of the ethnicity, conquering Uruk, where he established his capital.

swap.leadin: The largest remains of one of these structures can be found at Chonga Zanbil, which was built by the Elamites.
swap.text: Name these terraced religious buildings. A seven-storied example called the Etemenanki, which was dedicated to the god Marduk, got a reference in Herodotus's histories.
swap.clue: Koldewey also found one that he took to be a temple to Marduk, the name of which, Etemenanki, translates as "The Foundation of Heaven and Earth."

question.leadin: Answer these questions about an ancient empire.
question.text: reached its full glory under what last great Assyrian emperor? This son of Esar-Haddon ruled until approximately 633 BC.
question.clue: This ruler had to replace the king of Babylon after his brother Shamash-shum-ukin revolted.

swap.text: Following the battle, Alexander entered this city through its Ishtar gate. He would later die of unknown causes at this city in 323 BC.
swap.clue: This city's patron deity was worshipped in the Esagila.

question.text: The best example of a Sumerian schoolhouse was found in this city, which was the center of worship for Enlil. This city's Ekur Temple was rebuilt by Naram-Sin.
question.clue: Fragments of Hammurabi's Code have been found in this city, whose "scribal corner" is rich with ancient texts. Various Mesopotamian dynasties sought to control this city of religious importance, the home of the god Enlil.

swap.leadin: In Women of Babylon, Zainab Bahrani argues that Mesopotamian votive statues acted as portraits by referencing an alabaster disc depicting this ruler's daughter overseeing the pouring of a libation.
swap.text: Name this ruler, whose daughter Enheduanna was both a poet and high priestess to the god Nanna. This former cupbearer to Ur-Zababa of Kish was raised by the gardener Akki, who had found him floating in a river.
swap.clue: After taking Kish from Lugulzaggesi, he built his empire by extending trade from his capital city throughout to Susa and the Zagros mountains.

question.leadin: Objects such as an axe with a copper and gold handle adorned with a boar attest to the influence of these people's culture in Ugarit.
question.text: Name these people whose namesake language was primarily spoken in the Mitanni kingdom.
question.clue: This ethnic group largely made up the population of the Mitanni Kingdom to the southeast of the Hittite Empire. Kikkuli ("kee-KOO-lee") wrote a horse training manual in this ethnic group's namesake language, which was most closely related to Urartian.

swap.text: In its later years, Hittite foreign policy included maintaining the existence of this empire, with capital at Washukanni, as a buffer state between the Hittites and Assyria. This state's conquest by Adad-Nirari I put Hittite national security in great peril.
swap.clue: Based on terms in the Kikkuli horse-training manual, the names of several rulers, and a list of deities found in a treaty, the rulers of this polity are argued to have been Indo-Europeans.

question.leadin: This city was captured by the Gutians, who came out of the Zagros Mountains in 2180 BCE.
question.text: Name this capital city of a namesake dynasty, founded in the twenty-fourth century BCE.
question.clue: Its exact location is unknown, but is believed to be somewhere on the east bank of the Tigris.

swap.leadin: Dominant rulers gradually claimed this title instead of ensi, which kings of Isin and Larsa took as pious stewards of a temple's farmlands.
swap.text: Give this Sumerian title that precedes "Anne-Mundu" to identify a "king of the four corners" from Adab, "Zage-Si" to identify a warlord overthrown by Sargon, and "banda" to identify a mythical king of Uruk.

question.leadin: Answer the following about Larsa, the city which supplanted Isin as the strongest power in lower Mesopotamia before being conquered by Hammurabi.
question.text: Larsa attained independence from Isin under the governor Gungunum, who was of this ethnicity. Hammurabi belonged to this ethnicity, whose members ruled Babylon before the Kassites and Elamites.
question.clue: This Semitic people who established the cities of Ebla and Mari while usurping cities like Kish and Eshnunna. The most famous member of this people conquered Larsa from Rim-Sin I and also instituted a draconian law code demanding "an eye for an eye."

swap.leadin: The only woman attested to in this document is Kug-Bu, the Tavern Keeper.
swap.text: Name this compendium of rulers that includes five dynasties of Kish and three dynasties of Ur.
